transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-29
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO, Trident), Sara Gomez (ML Eng), Evan Liu (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Trident is running most prototypes on OpenAI; experimenting with vLLM/TGI for cost savings. They need parity on our evals, clear latency/cost numbers, and assurance around data security (VPC/KMS). Agreed next step: 2-week pilot to run benchmarks and compare p95/p99 latency, token cost, and quality regressions.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. Luis will do the deep dive. Ravi, Sara, Evan — thanks for making time.
[00:00:18] Ravi: Thanks Maya. Wanted to get a sense for where Redwood fits in our serving strategy. We're currently prototyping with OpenAI for quality and also running some local experiments with vLLM/TGI to reduce spend.
[00:00:36] Luis: Got it. Quick question up front — is the priority cost first, or do you need identical output to OpenAI as a hard requirement?
[00:00:49] Sara: Short answer: parity matters for a subset of prompts. We have evaluation suites that flag regressions. If latency drops or cost drops but accuracy regresses we lose product trust.
[00:01:05] Evan: Also infra constraints — anything that needs to live VPC/on-prem for data residency. We have PHI-ish data in some flows; need to be careful.
[00:01:20] Maya: Understood. We'll talk Hosted, Dedicated, Private and tradeoffs. Also, Luis will share a concrete benchmarking plan.
[00:01:37] Luis: Cool. Architecture wise, Redwood Hosted gives you fastest time-to-value; Dedicated is reserved capacity with predictable throughput; Private gives a customer-controlled control plane and VPC options. For parity, we usually run a short eval where we replicate your prompt sets and measure output-level metrics and token-level economics.
[00:02:04] Ravi: When you say replicate, how do you handle OpenAI model names? We currently use a mix — some GPT-4-ish proprietary model via vendor and some Claude-ish tests.
[00:02:20] Luis: We map to verified open model variants in our catalog; sometimes that means moving to LlamaX-like weights or other community models. For immediate parity we can also run hosted endpoints that are compatible with the same decode settings — temperature, top-p, stop sequences — to reduce diffs. There's occasional tokenization differences which can affect exact outputs.
[00:02:46] Sara: Tokenization differences are a pain. Our eval harness complains when the prompt + delimiter tokenize differently. Can you reproduce tokenization behavior exactly?
[00:02:57] Luis: Not always exact matching with OpenAI's BPEs, but we can normalize at the harness level and measure semantic parity (ROUGE/F1/embedding similarity). We'll also run unit tests for hallucination rate on your golden set.
[00:03:20] Ravi: Good. On infra, Evan — we may need a Private deployment for certain regulated workflows. What's involved?
[00:03:29] Evan: If we need VPC and KMS integration, we'd need customer-managed keys and an audit log for access. Also SSO for RBAC.
[00:03:38] Maya: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations and a private control plane. We support SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs in the console. Our SOC2 report and the security pack cover retention and access controls — we'll share those docs.
[00:03:55] Evan: Great. What's the typical uplift in cost/complexity between Dedicated and Private?
[00:04:04] Luis: Dedicated is basically reserved GPU pools we manage but isolated to your tenant — lower ops on your side. Private (VPC/on-prem) adds more setup and networking complexity and the license/engagement overhead. We can put numbers in a pricing sheet for a 1-2 GPU pod vs a dedicated fleet.
[00:04:27] Ravi: Latency constraints: for our customer-facing assistant we want sub-200ms p95 for short completion tasks (<= 64 tokens). Does Redwood have data on p95 for those configs?
[00:04:39] Luis: On modern A100/RTX setups with optimized kernels and KV cache warm, we regularly see <= 200ms p95 for small seq lengths on batch sizes tuned for latency. We'll include sample benchmarks. Note: batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency; we tune per-route.
[00:05:02] Sara: We're also looking at quantized models for cost. Does Redwood support 4-bit/8-bit quantization and how does that affect quality?
[00:05:12] Luis: Yes, runtime supports quantized execution paths. We recommend running your evaluation harness with quantization profiles — Redwood Optimize will suggest profiles based on your workload. In many cases 4-bit QAT/LLM quant gives big cost wins with minimal quality drop, but we need your evals to confirm.
[00:05:36] Ravi: On the vLLM/TGI experiments we ran locally, we saw weird KV cache behavior under long convo contexts — sometimes the perf drops unexpectedly. Can Redwood reproduce and how do you manage KV cache?
[00:05:48] Luis: The runtime has explicit KV cache management and continuous batching that does a lot of heavy lifting. If you're hitting pathological sequences we'll instrument the KV hit/miss rate and tune the caching TTLs. We'll replicate with your context lengths in the pilot.
[00:06:08] Evan: For the pilot, what do you need from us to get started?
[00:06:13] Maya: We'll need your representative prompt set, expected success metrics, and a rough daily token volume. We'll propose a benchmark harness and a two-week run with p95/p99 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and semantic parity scores.
[00:06:29] Ravi: Token volumes are modest to start — ~100k tokens/day for experiments but we want to plan for scale to 2-3M tokens/day by Q1.
[00:06:39] Sara: We'll share our eval suite; it has unit tests and rollout tests for hallucination.
[00:06:45] Luis: Perfect. We'll run three modes: Hosted Redwood endpoints, Dedicated config sized to your expected throughput, and a Private (if you opt in) staging deployment to assess networking overhead.
[00:07:02] Maya: One thing to call out — compatibility shims for folks moving from OpenAI are common. We provide a thin compatibility layer for request/response shapes to minimize app changes.
[00:07:15] Ravi: Nice. Any gotchas people typically see when porting from Azure OpenAI?
[00:07:21] Luis: Two common ones: tokenization and supported system prompts/stop token semantics. Also, rate limits and retry semantics can differ. We document them and include a migration checklist.
[00:07:34] Sara: Does Redwood support function-calling style structured outputs? We rely on structured JSON responses for downstream processing.
[00:07:42] Luis: Yes — we support streaming, structured output, and function/tool calling patterns. We'll validate the JSON schema preservation during the pilot.
[00:07:55] Evan: Security again — you mentioned audit logs. Are logs stored in Redwood or can they be forwarded to our SIEM?
[00:08:03] Maya: Both. We provide audit logs in the console and can stream events to your SIEM (S3/Kinesis/CloudWatch options) for enterprise accounts.
[00:08:13] Ravi: Great. Let's talk numbers briefly — what's the pricing model for Hosted vs Dedicated?
[00:08:20] Maya: Hosted is usage-based (per-token + embeddings units), Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commits and an option to burst. Private has a platform fee. We'll send a tailored pricing sheet after we scope the pilot.
[00:08:38] Sara: For the evaluation, will Redwood run the helm of the harness or do we run it and give you results?
[00:08:45] Luis: We can run it both ways. Often customers share the harness and we run to ensure reproducibility; we also provide the harness so you can run locally. For parity we recommend both to cross-validate.
[00:09:00] Ravi: Any concerns about compliance — HIPAA-ish data?
[00:09:05] Maya: We have customers with PHI requirements; Private deployments or Dedicated with appropriate BAAs are the usual approaches. We'll share the compliance pack and an outline for BAAs.
[00:09:18] Evan: Network egress — for Private we want traffic to stay within VPC where possible. Is that doable?
[00:09:25] Luis: Yes, Private supports VPC peering and on-prem connectors so you can keep traffic internal and integrate with your KMS/HSM.
[00:09:34] Speaker 1: (inaudible) question about model updates and rollouts.
[00:09:40] Luis: Rollouts are in the console — canary, A/B, automatic fallback to compatible variants. You can pin model versions to routes. We'll also surface eval regressions tied to your prompt sets.
[00:09:56] Sara: For canaries, can we test only a segment of users and shift traffic gradually?
[00:10:02] Maya: Yes — percent-based rollouts are supported and we can automate rollback if quality metrics drop.
[00:10:10] Ravi: Any examples of customers who migrated from Anthropic or Azure and saw cost/latency wins?
[00:10:18] Maya: We have anonymized case notes — a fintech customer moved from an expensive hosted vendor to Dedicated and halved token costs while keeping p95 latency similar. We'll include a short anonymized case study.
[00:10:33] Evan: On the operational side, how do we get alerted to regressions?
[00:10:37] Luis: Redwood Optimize ties to your evals and can alert on quality regressions. The console has traces and token-level cost breakdowns.
[00:10:47] Sara: Are there SDKs we need to change? We currently use an OpenAI-compatible SDK.
[00:10:53] Maya: The API is OpenAI-compatible for common patterns; SDKs are available and we document the mapping and any differences.
[00:11:04] Ravi: About the pilot — what metrics will make this a success for Trident?
[00:11:08] Sara: Semantic parity within 2-3% of our current F1/ROUGE on the golden set, p95 latency under 200ms for short queries, and cost per 1k tokens reduced by at least 20% on Dedicated.
[00:11:24] Luis: Makes sense. We'll instrument and report those.
[00:11:29] Maya: We'll put this into an official pilot plan and share docs.
[00:11:34] Ravi: A couple of technical clarifications — you mentioned quantization profiles. Do you do QAT or post-training quantization?
[00:11:42] Luis: We support multiple quant paths depending on the model. For community models we often use post-training quant but can recommend QAT for best fidelity if you can fine-tune. We'll detail tradeoffs.
[00:11:58] Sara: Does Redwood maintain its own kernel library for attention ops?
[00:12:02] Luis: Yes — the runtime chooses optimized kernels at serving time based on model arch and sequence lengths. That helps with consistent latency.
[00:12:12] Evan: Any specifics about handling long conversation histories and cache eviction?
[00:12:16] Luis: We'll record KV cache hit/miss and provide tuning knobs — TTLs, segmenting long histories, and prefix caching for common system prompts.
[00:12:27] Ravi: Can we test both streaming and non-streaming modes? Our frontend relies on streaming for perceived latency.
[00:12:33] Luis: Absolutely — we'll include streaming p95 and end-to-end render times in the harness.
[00:12:41] Sara: One last product question — is model compilation performed ahead of time or JIT at first request?
[00:12:47] Luis: There's a warmup/compilation step; we cache compiled kernels for subsequent requests. For Dedicated you can pin warm instances so cold starts aren't visible.
[00:12:59] Maya: Okay — want to quick recap and next steps so we leave with clarity?
[00:13:04] Ravi: Yes please.
[00:13:06] Maya: Recap: Redwood will send security/compliance pack and pricing sheet. SE will prepare benchmark harness and run three configs (Hosted, Dedicated, Private staging). Trident to share prompt set and success metrics. Proposed pilot week: 2025-09-08 kickoff and two-week run.
[00:13:26] Sara: Sounds good. We'll prioritize the prompts and the eval pass.
[00:13:30] Evan: I'll check internal KMS and VPC constraints and confirm by early next week.
[00:13:36] Maya: Great, action items recorded. Any other questions?
[00:13:40] Ravi: None from me. Thanks all.
[00:13:43] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the attachments.

(remaining ~39 minutes of the meeting were used for a live architecture Q&A and some screen-sharing where Luis stepped through a sample benchmark harness and an anonymized case study; transcription quality drops a bit during screen-share and some lines are partial)

[00:22:00] Luis: (screen-share) here's a sample harness — it's a small python runner that emits requests at controlled qps and records latency histograms, token counts and similarity scores. We also seed with your gold prompts.
[00:22:24] Sara: Looks good; can we add a hallucination unit test that checks extraneous facts?
[00:22:31] Luis: Yes, we can plug that in.
[00:27:05] Maya: Quick side note — for customers trying to replicate vLLM on-prem results we sometimes see differences due to different CUDA/kernels; that's expected. We'll help tune it.
[00:35:10] Ravi: One last nuance — our legal team will ask about data deletion and logs after pilot completion.
[00:35:18] Maya: We'll include data retention and deletion procedures in the security pack.
[00:40:00] Luis: We're capturing the telemetry we'll need to show parity and will push a baseline report after the pilot.
[00:45:30] Sara: Thanks — appreciate the thoroughness.
[00:51:50] Maya: Closing — we will send docs and calendar invite for kickoff. Thanks everyone.

Action items (auto):
